overview: This “Mongols” record covers 1100 to 1200, before the Mongol Empire formed. It concerns communities and competing leaders of the eastern steppe, including Temujin’s rise. Its enormous imported outline stretches far into northeastern Asia and cannot be treated as a unified Mongol state or an ethnic boundary. The atlas changes labels around 1200; the conventional imperial founding belongs to 1206.

periods.title: Khitan frontier world
periods.summary: Mongol communities lived within a wider landscape shaped by Khitan power.

periods.title: Competing leaders and alliances
periods.summary: The collapse of Khitan rule opened a period of shifting steppe politics.

periods.title: Toward imperial unification
periods.summary: Temujin’s alliance with the Jin preceded the new imperial order.

items.text: Temujin’s early task was to gather scattered followers of his Borjigid lineage and build authority among neighboring groups. Tatars, Kereyit, Naiman and Merkit had their own leaders and interests. Creating a larger coalition involved bargaining, loyalty and warfare. The later empire should not be projected backward onto this divided landscape.

In 1196, Temujin fought on the Jin dynasty’s side against the Tatars near the Ulz River. His contribution helped him gain Jin support and strengthen his own position. The future conqueror of northern China was, at this stage, cooperating with one of its ruling dynasties. Political relationships could change dramatically within a generation.

The Serven Khaalga monument preserves Chinese and Jurchen inscriptions recording places passed by the Jin army. Researchers compared those names with geography and archaeological evidence to reconstruct its 1196 route. This discovery gives a check on later stories about the region. The languages belong to the Jin record; they are not evidence of a twelfth-century Mongolian inscription.

sections.title: Family work, friendship and moving camp

items.text: The later Secret History remembers Temujin’s mother, Hö’elün, feeding her abandoned family with gathered fruits and roots. Her sons learned to catch fish. The episode places a mother’s knowledge and hard work at the center of survival. It is a retrospective family story, not a typical menu for every household.

The same chronicle recalls young Temujin and Jamukha exchanging knucklebones and playing on river ice. Later they practiced archery and exchanged arrowheads, including one made to whistle. Their childhood games became part of a story about sworn friendship. Imagine a present that made a noise as it flew!

A black sable coat appears in the chronicle as a wedding gift from Börte’s family. Temujin then presented it to To’oril, an ally of his father, seeking support. A valuable garment could warm a body and help build a political relationship. Family celebrations and diplomacy were closely connected.

Another scene follows a moving camp with carts, horse-herders, shepherds and lamb-herds. Börte interprets Jamukha’s remarks as a warning and urges the household to move away. The narrative gives her political judgment an important role. Looking after a mobile household included decisions about people and alliances as well as animals.

sections.title: A rare archaeological glimpse of the region

items.text: At Khar Nuur in eastern Mongolia, archaeologists found a woman’s burial inserted into an older frontier enclosure. Combined radiocarbon results place it between 1158 and 1214, with uncertainty spanning the empire’s beginning. It reveals a community in the region of Mongol emergence; her precise political or ethnic affiliation remains unidentified.

Her grave contained gold ornaments, a silver cup and fine silk. Examined fabric bundles used high-quality reeled threads and included blue, red, brown and cream colors. Researchers think the silk probably came from China. These materials show connections beyond the grasslands, though one wealthy burial cannot tell us how ordinary families dressed.

The woman was estimated to have died between forty and sixty. Her skeleton showed joint and spinal changes suggesting an active life, and she had lost almost all her teeth before death. Chewing was probably difficult. The evidence brings physical strain into view, but does not reveal what treatment or assistance she received.

An earlier regional comparison comes from Site 23, a Liao frontier garrison with a rubbish deposit dated around 1050. Its animal bones include sheep, goats, cattle, horses and dogs, alongside wild animals and Amur catfish. Frontier subsistence combined herding with hunting and fishing. These remains predate this map period and should not be assigned automatically to Mongol households.

sections.title: How the stories survived, and a later written voice

items.text: The Secret History is a thirteenth-century Mongolian work blending family history, poetry, speeches and political narrative. Its original manuscript is lost; scholars reconstruct its wording from later copies using Chinese characters to record Mongolian sounds. The vivid childhood scenes therefore arrive through literary composition and manuscript transmission, rather than through surviving twelfth-century notebooks.

A later, securely dated comparison is Töregene’s edict of 1240. Its Mongolian portion begins, in Igor de Rachewiltz’s normalized Roman reading, “Ene minu üge”: “This is my word”, meaning an order. Three Mongolian lines follow a longer Chinese text. The phrase illustrates early imperial written authority after this card’s period. Its Roman transcription represents Mongolian writing; the punctuation is editorial.

ending.text: Temujin’s recognition as Chinggis Khan in 1206 marked a new imperial political order. Earlier communities were incorporated and reorganized rather than disappearing. The map’s 1200 endpoint and later empire label divide the dataset, not the lives of Mongol families.
